ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The trial was reviewed and approved by BeyondBound IRB: BB2511NC-152, and registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT07431840).
Recruitment outreach consisted of IRB-approved advertising by email, digital marketing channels and word of mouth.
The IRB-approved study landing page hosted on the People Science website led to an IRB-approved pre-screening questionnaire to determine individual qualification.
This study was reviewed and approved by BeyondBound IRB BB2511NC-152, and all participants gave informed consent.
table.header: Ethics Approval and Consent to Participate

table.text: Eligible participants were adults aged 60 years or older who experienced upper respiratory symptoms (i.e., coughing, sneezing, or congestion) at least two to three times during the cold and flu season and were able to read and understand English.
Participants were required to provide informed consent, use a personal smartphone and download the Consumer Health Learning & Organizing Ecosystem (Chloe) by People Science app.
table.formatted: Participants were required to provide informed consent, use a personal smartphone and download the Consumer Health Learning & Organizing Ecosystem (Chloe) by People Science app.

table.text: Participants were also ineligible if they had other underlying conditions or comorbidities that could confound the study outcomes, used cannabis-or nicotine-containing products daily, had known hypersensitivity to milk products, sorbitol, or tableting aids, or were judged by the principal investigator to be unable to comply with, or unsuitable for, the study.

Following screening and eligibility confirmation, participants were randomized in a blinded fashion to one of three arms (Placebo, 50 mg IDP, or 200 mg IDP) and were shipped study product within two weeks before the baseline period.

During the one-week baseline period, participants completed a quality-of-life survey and were asked daily whether they had upper respiratory symptoms, completing the WURSS-24 along with rescue-medication and dailyactivity questions when symptoms were present.
Recruitment, Consent, and Enrollment Participants were recruited through social media channels and researcher networks.

Qualified participants were invited to download the Chloe application (described below) and create an account to access the Informed Consent Form and continue through eligibility determination and enrollment.

The daily survey covered general wellbeing and presence of upper respiratory symptoms; when symptoms were present, participants completed the WURSS-24 and additional questions on rescue-medication use and impact on daily activities.

Each day, participants were asked whether they had any upper respiratory symptoms and, if so, completed the Wisconsin Upper Respiratory Symptom Survey (WURSS-24), rating symptom severity and functional impact.
Adverse Events Participants were prompted weekly to disclose any adverse events that occurred.
This study was reviewed and approved by BeyondBound IRB BB2511NC-152, and all participants gave informed consent.
table.header: Ethics Approval and Consent to Participate

table.text: Recruitment and Conduct Participants were recruited from December 1st, 2025-March 1st, 2026, through social media and researcher networks and completed all study activities remotely using the Chloe app.
At each allocation, Chloe compared the cumulative proportion of participants assigned to each arm against its target and assigned the participant to the first arm that was below its target.
Participants were enrolled formally by blinded study coordinators following randomization.

Sample Size, Compliance and Demographics Of 281 participants who were randomized, 265 completed the study and 16 were withdrawn due to loss to follow-up (7), participant decision (7), and investigator or other decision (2) (Figure 1).
N=255 participants were evaluable based on sufficient baseline and end of study data and analyzed.
The trial was concluded when all randomized, non-withdrawn participants completed the study. 2).
table.formatted: The trial was concluded when all randomized, non-withdrawn participants completed the study.  <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

table.text: Data on symptom trajectories were additionally segregated by whether participants were asymptomatic at baseline, but no statistical group differences were noted (data not shown).

Upper respiratory symptom burden declined markedly from baseline through the product-use period across the cohort as a whole, as expected for participants enrolled during peak symptom season and followed as the season recedes, and potentially further amplified by regression to the mean among individuals who joined the study while symptomatic.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p>0.05", "p<0.05", "p>0.05", "p > 0.05", 
"p>0.05", "p>0.05", "p<0.05"), Text = c("Groups did not differ significantly at baseline on age, sex, or race/ethnicity (all Fisher's Exact Test p>0.05).", 
"However, area under the curve of cough and chest congestion prevalence and severity were reduced at a significantly greater rate in the pooled 50 mg IDP® + 200 mg IDP® group (MWU BH-FDR p<0.05 for both measures, weeks 1-8 of product use, respectively) (Figure 3).", 
"IDP® doses did not differ from one another (MWU p>0.05).", 
"Overall, 43 of the randomized participants (15.3%) reported at least one 317 adverse event (68 events total), with no significant between-arm difference in the proportion 318 reporting an AE (p > 0.05). 3 serious adverse events were reported but not considered possibly 319 related to study product use: a fall down the stairs and an Achilles tendon tear at different times 320 in the same individual (200 mg IDP), and an episode of vertigo determined to be caused by 321 displaced otoliths (50 mg IDP).", 
"481 Group % Flu Vaccine Last Year % Flu Vaccine Ever Placebo 47.7 76.1 50 mg IDP 50.6 69.4 200 mg IDP 58.5 76.8 FET p>0.05 in all cases 482 483 Other Vaccinations, by Group 484", 
"ANCOVA p>0.05 and MMRM p>0.05 for all metrics.", "MWU 301 indicates that the pooled 50 mg IDP® + 200 mg IDP® group has significantly lower area AUC 302 for chest congestion and cough prevalence and severity (MWU FDR-BH p<0.05 for all)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p>0.05", "p>0.05", "p=0.97 ", "p=0.67", "p > 0.05", "p=1.0", "p>0.05 ", "p>0.05 ", "p>0.05 "), Sentence = c("Groups did not differ significantly at baseline on age, sex, or race/ethnicity (all Fisher's Exact Test p>0.05).", "IDP® doses did not differ from one another (MWU p>0.05).", "There was no difference between the 50mg and 200 mg doses for either symptom (cough MWU p=0.97 and chest congestion MWU p=0.67).", "There was no difference between the 50mg and 200 mg doses for either symptom (cough MWU p=0.97 and chest congestion MWU p=0.67).", "Overall, 43 of the randomized participants (15.3%) reported at least one 317 adverse event (68 events total), with no significant between-arm difference in the proportion 318 reporting an AE (p > 0.05). 3 serious adverse events were reported but not considered possibly 319 related to study product use: a fall down the stairs and an Achilles tendon tear at different times 320 in the same individual (200 mg IDP), and an episode of vertigo determined to be caused by 321 displaced otoliths (50 mg IDP).", "Group COV ID-19 Pneumococcal (Pneumonia) Shingles (Zoster) Tetanus/Diphtheria/Pertussis (Tdap) Measles/Mumps/Rubella (MMR) Hepatitis B Other Placebo 32 (36.4%) 12 (13.6%) 8 (9.1%) 1 (1.1%) 2 (2.3%) 1 (1.1%) 46 (52.3 %) 50 mg IDP 31 (36.5%) 12 (14.1%) 12 (14.1 %) 8 (9.4%) 3 (3.5%) 1 (1.2%) 38 (44.7 %) 200 mg IDP 37 (45.1%) 12 (14.6%) 8 (9.8%) 7 (8.5%) 4 (4.9%) 3 (3.7%) 41 (50.0 %) However, Tetanus/Diphtheria/Pertussis (Tdap) vaccination was significantly more common in 486 both active-dose groups than in Placebo (Placebo 1.1% [1/88] vs. 50 mg IDP® 9.4% [8/85], 487 FDR p=0.045; ethics_statements: The trial was reviewed and approved by BeyondBound IRB: BB2511NC-152, and registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT07431840).
Recruitment outreach consisted of IRB-approved advertising by email, digital marketing channels and word of mouth.
The IRB-approved study landing page hosted on the People Science website led to an IRB-approved pre-screening questionnaire to determine individual qualification.
This study was reviewed and approved by BeyondBound IRB BB2511NC-152, and all participants gave informed consent.
live_data_statements: Eligible participants were adults aged 60 years or older who experienced upper respiratory symptoms (i.e., coughing, sneezing, or congestion) at least two to three times during the cold and flu season and were able to read and understand English.
Participants were required to provide informed consent, use a personal smartphone and download the Consumer Health Learning & Organizing Ecosystem (Chloe) by People Science app.

Participants were also ineligible if they had other underlying conditions or comorbidities that could confound the study outcomes, used cannabis-or nicotine-containing products daily, had known hypersensitivity to milk products, sorbitol, or tableting aids, or were judged by the principal investigator to be unable to comply with, or unsuitable for, the study.

Following screening and eligibility confirmation, participants were randomized in a blinded fashion to one of three arms (Placebo, 50 mg IDP, or 200 mg IDP) and were shipped study product within two weeks before the baseline period.

During the one-week baseline period, participants completed a quality-of-life survey and were asked daily whether they had upper respiratory symptoms, completing the WURSS-24 along with rescue-medication and dailyactivity questions when symptoms were present.
Recruitment, Consent, and Enrollment Participants were recruited through social media channels and researcher networks.

Qualified participants were invited to download the Chloe application (described below) and create an account to access the Informed Consent Form and continue through eligibility determination and enrollment.

The daily survey covered general wellbeing and presence of upper respiratory symptoms; when symptoms were present, participants completed the WURSS-24 and additional questions on rescue-medication use and impact on daily activities.

Each day, participants were asked whether they had any upper respiratory symptoms and, if so, completed the Wisconsin Upper Respiratory Symptom Survey (WURSS-24), rating symptom severity and functional impact.
Adverse Events Participants were prompted weekly to disclose any adverse events that occurred.
This study was reviewed and approved by BeyondBound IRB BB2511NC-152, and all participants gave informed consent.

Recruitment and Conduct Participants were recruited from December 1st, 2025-March 1st, 2026, through social media and researcher networks and completed all study activities remotely using the Chloe app.
At each allocation, Chloe compared the cumulative proportion of participants assigned to each arm against its target and assigned the participant to the first arm that was below its target.
Participants were enrolled formally by blinded study coordinators following randomization.

Sample Size, Compliance and Demographics Of 281 participants who were randomized, 265 completed the study and 16 were withdrawn due to loss to follow-up (7), participant decision (7), and investigator or other decision (2) (Figure 1).
N=255 participants were evaluable based on sufficient baseline and end of study data and analyzed.
The trial was concluded when all randomized, non-withdrawn participants completed the study. 2).
Data on symptom trajectories were additionally segregated by whether participants were asymptomatic at baseline, but no statistical group differences were noted (data not shown).

Upper respiratory symptom burden declined markedly from baseline through the product-use period across the cohort as a whole, as expected for participants enrolled during peak symptom season and followed as the season recedes, and potentially further amplified by regression to the mean among individuals who joined the study while symptomatic.
